question: Can recurrent transformer solvers enforce equivariance to interchangeable digits or colors architecturally, reduce permutation augmentation, and extrapolate across symbol-set and grid sizes without sacrificing exact task performance or computational practicality?

key_findings.claim: SE-RRM makes ordinary symbols an explicit tensor axis and alternates attention over positions and symbols, yielding exact symbol-permutation equivariance for the restricted architecture in Proposition 2.3.
key_findings.evidence: Each ordinary symbol uses the same D-vector, absence uses zero, and the state has shape D by I by K. Every block applies position-axis attention, symbol-axis attention, and token-wise normalization/MLP; a one-logit-per-symbol output preserves the axis action. The theorem excludes task-type embeddings and assumes the uniformly shared construction, so it is not an unconditional guarantee for every deployed configuration.

key_findings.claim: The abstract's blanket architectural guarantee is qualified by task-type and special-symbol pathways that can intentionally break the full symbol permutation group.
key_findings.evidence: Task-type embeddings are initialized identically across K but are allowed to deviate during learning, explicitly to handle task types where symbol equivariance is inappropriate; Proposition 2.3 therefore states 'without task-type embeddings.' Special mask/unknown symbols also receive distinct vectors and are not interchangeable with usual symbols. ARC-AGI training uses task identifiers, so exact color-equivariance of the trained ARC system is not formally established by the proposition.

key_findings.claim: On in-distribution 9x9 Sudoku, the 2M-parameter SE-RRM substantially exceeds the reproduced HRM and TRM exact-solve rates.
key_findings.evidence: With 16 deep-supervision steps, SE-RRM obtains 93.73% FSR (95% Wilson interval 93.66-93.81) and 97.58% unfilled-cell accuracy. HRM obtains 63.53%/86.11% and the reproduced transformer TRM 71.94%/89.80%. The paper separately notes TRM's published fixed-size MLP-mixer result of 87.4%, which narrows but does not erase the in-distribution gap and cannot accept other grid sizes. The evaluation uses all 422,786 test puzzles, explaining narrow puzzle-level intervals, but reports no training-seed uncertainty.

key_findings.claim: Zero-shot generalization from 9x9 to 4x4 is strong, but the claimed extrapolation to 16x16 and 25x25 never produces a completely correct puzzle.
key_findings.evidence: SE-RRM solves 95.46% of 288 4x4 puzzles and reaches 99.15% cell accuracy. On 216 16x16 puzzles it has 0% FSR (upper Wilson bound 1.75%) and 51.95% cell accuracy; on only 42 curated 25x25 puzzles it has 0% FSR (upper bound 8.38%) and 31.49% cell accuracy. The larger-grid results show above-random partial predictions and interface compatibility, not successful exact solving.

key_findings.claim: Recurrent test-time scaling is unusually strong on 9x9 Sudoku for SE-RRM over the measured 1-128-step range.
key_findings.evidence: Exact solve rate rises from 16.05% at one deep-supervision step to 93.73% at 16, 98.22% at 64, and 98.84% at 128. At 128 steps HRM reaches 68.15% and TRM 79.78%. Main comparisons use 16 steps, and latency or FLOPs per step are not reported despite SE-RRM's more expensive state.

key_findings.claim: On ARC-AGI, SE-RRM is statistically compatible with TRM rather than demonstrably better, while using far fewer color augmentations.
key_findings.evidence: SE-RRM pass@2 is 45.3% (40.44-50.15) on ARC-AGI-1 and 7.1% (3.42-12.61) on ARC-AGI-2 versus TRM's 44.6% (39.71-49.40) and 7.8% (4.0-13.64); both interval pairs overlap heavily. SE-RRM uses 8 dihedral augmentations rather than the 1,000 augmentations reported for HRM/TRM. It exceeds HRM's 40.3% and 5.0%, but those intervals also overlap on ARC-AGI-1.

key_findings.claim: The ARC ablation supports a benefit from the combined symbol-axis architecture and matched recipe, but does not isolate equivariance alone.
key_findings.evidence: Starting from TRM at 44.6%, random halting drops to 34.8%, RoPE2D to 38.4%, both to 33.1%, and all SE-RRM hyperparameters matched to 32.3%. Adding the two-dimensional embedding and SE-RRM architecture then reaches 45.3%. Because the last step bundles tensorization, extra attention, output design, and equivariance, it cannot attribute the 13-point recovery specifically to symmetry.

anchors.section: Appendix D.1 / Table A5 ARC ablation

key_findings.claim: The cleanest Sudoku symmetry ablation shows a four-point exact-solve benefit, materially smaller than the full SE-RRM-versus-TRM gap.
key_findings.evidence: Within SE-RRM, shared symbol embeddings produce 93.7% 9x9 FSR while non-shared embeddings produce 89.7%; TRM is 71.9%. Thus enforced equivariance has direct positive evidence, but most of the 21.8-point headline gap can also involve tensorized representation, axial attention, training dynamics, and hyperparameters.

anchors.section: Appendix D.3 / Table A7 shared-embedding ablation

key_findings.claim: The paper contains important negative results showing that equivariance and recipe choices are task-conditional and brittle.
key_findings.evidence: For Maze, forcing symbol equivariance collapses SE-RRM from 88.8% FSR to 0%, so the deployed model deliberately breaks it. TRM with random halting plus RoPE2D also collapses to 0% Sudoku, whereas SE-RRM remains strong under several configurations. On SE-RRM itself, RoPE gives 95.4% Sudoku versus 93.7% for the main RoPE2D choice. These outcomes argue for symmetry selection and robust tuning, not a universally beneficial constraint.

anchors.section: Tables A6-A7 / zero-result and equivariance ablation

key_findings.claim: Parameter efficiency does not imply compute or memory efficiency because SE-RRM expands every position across K symbols.
key_findings.evidence: With efficient attention, the paper gives time O(I^2 K + K^2 I) and memory O(IK), versus O(I^2) and O(I) for the vanilla attention sequence, describing an approximately linear factor-K increase when I is much larger than K and impractical K^2 I cost when K dominates. No measured latency, peak memory, energy, or equal-FLOP accuracy accompanies the 2M-versus-7M/27M parameter comparison.

anchors.section: Appendix C / model sizes and batch sizes

key_findings.claim: The Maze result demonstrates architectural applicability after symmetry is disabled, but cannot validate symbol equivariance.
key_findings.evidence: The non-equivariant SE-RRM scores 88.8% FSR (86.64-90.65), TRM 85.3% (82.92-87.41), and HRM 74.5% (71.66-77.15). The SE-RRM/TRM intervals overlap, and the paper itself proposes the higher-dimensional embedding or extra transformer layer—not symmetry—as possible explanations.

key_findings.claim: Reported confidence intervals quantify puzzle sampling, not model-training reproducibility or hyperparameter-selection uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: Tables use Wilson intervals over exact-solve or cell outcomes, but no independent training seeds or run-to-run variation are stated. Because the appendix exposes severe recipe interactions—including a 0% TRM configuration—single-training-run comparisons can understate uncertainty in architecture-level conclusions.

method.core_idea: Represent a structured task as a D-by-position-by-symbol tensor with shared embeddings for interchangeable symbols, then apply recurrent transformer blocks that attend axially over positions and symbols so the symbol permutation acts by reindexing a network axis.
method.mechanism: For each position-symbol pair, the embedding is a shared learned vector when that symbol is present and zero otherwise, with separate vectors for noninterchangeable special tokens. Position and optional task-type embeddings are added. Each recurrent block applies self-attention along I, self-attention along K, and a feature MLP with token-wise RMS normalization and residuals. A shared projection from D to one logit produces an I-by-K output. Deep supervision trains repeated recurrent refinement; SE-RRM uses stochastic termination during training and the full chosen number of steps at inference. Sudoku, ARC-AGI, and Maze compare the architecture with HRM and TRM, with symmetry intentionally disabled on Maze.
assumptions: The relevant digits or colors are genuinely interchangeable under a full permutation group; special symbols and semantically distinct Maze tokens are excluded.
A shared embedding and uniformly applied axial operations are sufficient to preserve the desired group action through every recurrent block and output head.
Task-type embeddings either remain symmetric or are omitted when an exact per-task symbol-equivariance guarantee is claimed.
Flattened grid position with RoPE2D supplies the spatial structure needed while symbol permutation acts only on the K axis.
Training on 1,000 9x9 Sudoku seeds with 1,000 augmentations is adequate to learn size-independent rules rather than dataset regularities.
Cell accuracy meaningfully measures partial large-grid extrapolation even when exact solved rate is zero.
Official or reproduced HRM/TRM results are comparable despite different widths, batches, learning rates, schedules, halting policies, epochs, and parameter counts.
Wilson intervals over puzzles are an adequate uncertainty summary despite the absence of training-seed replication.
Parameter count is an informative efficiency proxy despite the factor-K tensor expansion and extra symbol-axis attention.
The ARC task identifier and included evaluation examples do not leak solutions and preserve the intended generalization protocol.
Stochastic training termination is a suitable substitute for HRM/TRM's learned Q-halting policy when inference always executes the fixed maximum in main results.

techniques.role: Turns each candidate symbol into a reindexable tensor axis instead of a symbol-specific feature vector.
Prevents ordinary digit/color identity from creating learned asymmetries.
Alternates communication across positions and across symbols while preserving each axis's permutation action.
Maintains equivariance by applying identical feature transformations to every position-symbol token.
Projects every symbol token identically so output logits permute with the K axis.
Trains the same reasoning block across iterative refinements while detaching between supervised segments.
Terminates training supervision stochastically instead of learning HRM/TRM's Q-based stopping rule.
Encodes two-dimensional grid structure separately from symbol identity.
Evaluates one 9x9-trained network on 4x4, 16x16, and 25x25 position and symbol cardinalities.
Provides the closest within-architecture estimate of the effect of enforced symbol equivariance.
Measures exact-solve gains as the same learned block is iterated from one to 128 supervision steps.
Quantifies finite-puzzle uncertainty for exact solved rates and cell-level accuracy.

evaluations.metric: Fully solved rate and accuracy on initially empty cells with 95% Wilson intervals
evaluations.result: SE-RRM 93.73% FSR and 97.58% cell accuracy; TRM 71.94% and 89.80%; HRM 63.53% and 86.11%
evaluations.baseline: Reproduced HRM and TRM under their respective recipes

evaluations.setting: Zero-shot 4x4 Sudoku after training only on 9x9
evaluations.metric: Fully solved rate and empty-cell accuracy
evaluations.result: SE-RRM 95.46% and 99.15%; HRM/TRM 0% exact solves; GPT-OSS-20B 100% on the simpler 4x4 set

evaluations.metric: Fully solved rate and empty-cell accuracy
evaluations.result: 0% FSR at both sizes; 51.95% cell accuracy on 216 16x16 puzzles and 31.49% on 42 25x25 puzzles
evaluations.baseline: HRM/TRM cannot represent the unseen symbols; random cell choice would be much lower but is not tabulated

evaluations.metric: Fully solved rate from 1 to 128 deep-supervision steps

evaluations.baseline: HRM and TRM at the same number of recurrent supervision steps, not equal FLOPs

evaluations.baseline: Published HRM/TRM values using substantially heavier augmentation

evaluations.setting: Maze-hard with semantically distinct symbols and equivariance disabled
evaluations.metric: Fully solved rate with 95% Wilson intervals

limitations: Author-stated: experiments use only a 2M-parameter SE-RRM; reduced parameters may offset but do not remove increased compute and memory.
Author-stated: symbol-axis attention costs O(I^2 K + K^2 I) time and O(IK) memory, becoming impractical when K is large relative to I.
Author-stated: symbol equivariance is inappropriate on Maze and is deliberately broken by separate embeddings.
Reviewer-identified: the exact equivariance proposition excludes task-type embeddings, although ARC uses task identifiers whose K slices may diverge during learning.
Reviewer-identified: special symbols receive distinct embeddings, so the guarantee applies to a selected group of equivalent ordinary symbols rather than arbitrary permutations of all tokens.
Reviewer-identified: exact-solve rate is zero on both claimed larger-grid extrapolation sets; only partial cell accuracy extrapolates.
Reviewer-identified: the 25x25 test has only 42 selected puzzles, yielding an 8.38% upper Wilson bound for the observed zero solve rate.
Reviewer-identified: no training-seed replicates are reported; Wilson intervals over puzzles do not cover optimizer or initialization variance.
Reviewer-identified: model comparisons vary architecture, hidden size, layers, batch, epochs, learning rate, positional encoding, schedule, halting, and parameters, limiting causal attribution.
Reviewer-identified: the clean shared-embedding ablation explains four Sudoku FSR points, not the entire 21.8-point gap over TRM.
Reviewer-identified: parameter count is emphasized without measured FLOPs, latency, peak memory, throughput, or equal-compute accuracy.
Reviewer-identified: ARC intervals overlap TRM on both benchmarks, so the evidence supports augmentation-efficient parity rather than a clear performance win.
Reviewer-identified: training on all few-shot examples from evaluation puzzle types and learned task embeddings makes the ARC protocol task-conditioned rather than unseen-task extrapolation.
Reviewer-identified: all main inference uses the maximum 16 steps, so the architecture is not evaluated with calibrated adaptive stopping or cost-quality curves.
failure_modes: A purportedly interchangeable color has task-dependent semantics, so enforcing the full permutation group removes necessary distinctions.
Learned task-type embeddings drift apart across symbols and silently void exact equivariance in a multi-task deployment.
Special mask or unknown tokens are accidentally included in the permutation group despite having separate embeddings.
The K-axis tensor exceeds available memory or symbol attention dominates latency as the alphabet grows.
High cell accuracy on a larger Sudoku violates one or more global constraints in every puzzle, leaving exact solve rate at zero.
Size extrapolation depends on RoPE phase behavior or dataset regularities and fails on different aspect ratios, clue densities, or harder generators.
A new training seed or recipe produces a collapse like the 0% TRM random-halting/RoPE2D configuration.
The extra symbol-attention layer and larger token count, rather than symmetry, explain apparent gains at unequal compute.
The model continues improving with recurrent steps but consumes much more compute than HRM/TRM at the same step count.
ARC performance falls when color augmentation is removed for transformations not exactly represented by the assumed group.
An incorrect partial grid is overconfident, making SE-RRM unsuitable as a stand-alone solver without constraint checking or repair.
The fixed random training halt fails to allocate computation by instance difficulty and wastes full-step inference on easy cases.
reusable_insights: Turn an exchangeable output vocabulary into an explicit axis and use identical per-element operations so equivariance follows by construction.
State the exact symmetry group, excluding masks, roles, and task-dependent symbols rather than calling all tokens interchangeable.
Audit every auxiliary path—task embeddings, positional encodings, heads, normalization, halting—for whether it preserves the group action.
Report exact constraint satisfaction alongside local-cell accuracy; partial extrapolation and solved-task extrapolation are distinct claims.
Use shared-versus-separate embeddings inside the same architecture as the minimum causal ablation for an equivariance claim.
Compare recurrence depth at equal measured FLOPs or latency because a step in a tensor-expanded equivariant model is not cost-equivalent to a vanilla step.
Treat symmetry selection as task-specific: the Maze collapse is a useful diagnostic for an overly broad group.
Pair a neural equivariant predictor with a symbolic checker or repair solver when global validity is mandatory.
Separate parameter efficiency from activation-memory and attention-compute efficiency.
Include multiple training seeds when architecture recipes show catastrophic interactions.
Test unseen symbol cardinality and unseen position cardinality independently to determine which axis actually generalizes.
Use task identifiers only with a proven equivariant construction if an exact per-task guarantee is required.
open_questions: Can task-type conditioning be made exactly symbol-equivariant while still expressing task types whose valid symmetry is a subgroup?
What architectural or training change converts 51.95%/31.49% large-grid cell accuracy into nonzero exact solve rate?
How does SE-RRM compare with HRM, TRM, URM, and value-set-invariant GNN solvers at matched FLOPs, latency, memory, and seeds?
Does the four-point shared-embedding gain persist across clue densities, Sudoku generators, symbol alphabets, and training sizes?
Which components of the final ARC recovery—symbol tensorization, second attention axis, output head, or shared embedding—are individually necessary?
Can learned subgroup selection avoid the 0% Maze collapse while preserving exact symmetry where appropriate?
Will linear-in-K memory and K^2 I symbol attention remain tractable for large vocabularies or combinatorial domains?
How robust is size extrapolation to alternative positional encodings and grid shapes beyond square Sudoku?
Can calibrated constraint violations or symbolic repair provide a more informative large-grid metric than raw cell accuracy?
Does an adaptive halting policy preserve equivariance and improve the accuracy-cost frontier over fixed 16-128-step inference?
How much augmentation is still necessary for spatial, relational, and subgroup symmetries not captured by color permutations?
Do independent training seeds preserve the reported test-time scaling curve and ARC parity?

competitive_landscape.title: Hierarchical Reasoning Model
competitive_landscape.relationship: HRM establishes the deeply supervised recurrent latent-reasoning family and the Sudoku, Maze, and ARC-AGI protocols used by SE-RRM.
competitive_landscape.difference: HRM uses symbol-specific embeddings, two hierarchical recurrent modules, about 27M parameters, and augmentation rather than an exact symbol axis; SE-RRM's novelty is architectural symbol equivariance and cross-cardinality input/output handling, while the baseline differs in many training and compute variables.

competitive_landscape.title: Less is More: Recursive Reasoning with Tiny Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: TRM is the closest compact recursive baseline and the direct template for SE-RRM's recurrent cycles and deep supervision.
competitive_landscape.difference: TRM remains a fixed symbol-embedding sequence and cannot natively introduce unseen digits; SE-RRM lifts symbols to an attended axis and reduces parameters to 2M, but increases activation/attention cost and does not clearly beat TRM on ARC within uncertainty.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Models for Output-Space Invariance in Combinatorial Problems
competitive_landscape.relationship: This ICLR 2022 work already targets value-set invariance, explicitly including training on 9x9 Sudoku and solving 16x16 by converting values into binary decisions or value nodes in a recurrent relational/GNN solver.
competitive_landscape.difference: It sharply narrows any claim that SE-RRM is the first neural architecture to accommodate unseen symbols or cross-size Sudoku. SE-RRM's distinct contribution is a symbol-equivariant axial-attention construction inside modern RRMs, a formal block equivariance statement, and ARC-AGI evaluation; unlike that predecessor, its reported 16x16 exact-solve rate is zero.
competitive_landscape.source_version: OpenReview forum ibrUkC-pbis, ICLR 2022 Poster, published 2022-01-28, revision last modified 2025-10-12

competitive_landscape.title: Universal Reasoning Model
competitive_landscape.relationship: URM is a current recurrent-transformer alternative evaluated on the same ARC-AGI and Sudoku family, emphasizing recurrence, convolution, and truncated backpropagation rather than symbol symmetry.
competitive_landscape.difference: URM reports substantially higher ARC pass@1 values but offers no exact color-permutation or unseen-symbol guarantee; SE-RRM contributes symmetry-controlled augmentation and cardinality transfer, so performance leadership and equivariance novelty are separate axes.

competitive_landscape.title: Investigating Design Choices for Recurrent Reasoning Models on 2D Tasks
competitive_landscape.relationship: This direct RRM analysis tests simpler recurrent-transformer variants on Sudoku and Maze and reports that basic design changes can greatly exceed the original HRM results.
competitive_landscape.difference: It narrows attribution of gains to any particular HRM/TRM recurrence design but retains ordinary symbol representations; SE-RRM contributes an explicit symbol group action and cardinality transfer, while its own comparisons likewise require component-matched and equal-compute ablations.
competitive_landscape.source_version: OpenReview forum cL840F9yoG, ICLR 2026 withdrawn submission, revision last modified 2026-02-12

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a new class of symbol-equivariant RRMs that guarantees identical outputs under digit/color permutations, needs far less augmentation, outperforms prior RRMs on Sudoku, and uniquely extrapolates from 9x9 to smaller and larger symbol/grid sizes.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The explicit K-axis construction and Proposition 2.3 support restricted exact equivariance; 9x9 and 4x4 exact-solve gains, ARC parity with 8 rather than 1,000 augmentations, strong recurrent scaling, and a shared-embedding ablation support practical value. Larger-grid evidence is only partial-cell accuracy with zero exact solves.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is axial symbol equivariance integrated into the HRM/TRM recurrent framework, not the first output-space-invariant neural combinatorial solver or the first system that can represent unseen Sudoku symbols. The earlier value-set-invariant GNN work already targets 9-to-16 Sudoku transfer. The guarantee must also be scoped to ordinary shared symbols and configurations without symmetry-breaking task embeddings; causal gains are four FSR points in the clean Sudoku ablation, while the remainder bundles architecture and recipe changes.

reviewer_notes: The index-pinned 18-page extraction was read end to end, including the full main paper, all references, Appendix A notation, Appendix B symmetry illustrations, every architecture/hyperparameter table in Appendix C, and every ARC, learning-dynamics, Sudoku, Maze, halting, positional-encoding, and enforced-equivariance ablation in Appendix D through page 18. The current Atom record is arXiv:2603.02193v1; the paper is the ICML 2026 PMLR 306 proceedings version. A fresh stream of the current arXiv PDF independently reproduced the indexed PDF SHA-256 5b7dfdc6474bb1060d7277677d7e17f8b7905b7a1fc4b2323a515ac1180ee058, and the cached extraction independently reproduced c4b9ab466cfee06b630b2f842b824262247c3f7315819b7e302d7daff12fa298. Five direct primary competitors were extensively checked at the exact records and versions listed on 2026-08-23. Author limits, reviewer limits, negative results, and internal qualifications are separated above. The central synthesis constraint is to distinguish architectural ability to ingest a new symbol count and above-random cell accuracy from successful exact extrapolation: the model solves no 16x16 or 25x25 test puzzle in the paper.
